title: Why Bowling is Awesome
summary: Josh and Chuck explain ten-pin bowling, a listener-suggested topic from Mark Bowles. They cover the basics of the game and frame scoring (strikes, spares, the perfect 300 game), the history of bowling balls from lignum wood through rubber, mineralite, plastic, and reactive resin, and how the 1990s ball changes sharply raised perfect-game counts. They discuss pins, lanes and lane oil patterns, bowling shoes, and the history of the automatic pin setter from pin boys through the American Machine and Foundry (AMF) machine, including how it works. The episode also covers bowling's history from ancient and medieval roots and the ten-pin origin rumor, the ABC, action bowling, and Don Carter's million-dollar contract, plus the decline and recent comeback of bowling, the seven-ten split, and a listener pronunciation tip about English county names ending in -shire.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener suggestion
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about doctors' names and introduce the topic, a listener suggestion from Mark Bowles about bowling's backstory.

segments.title: Describing ten-pin bowling
segments.summary: The hosts describe ten-pin bowling as an American invention, with pin arrangement, lane dimensions, the foul line, gutters, and the pocket. They also discuss personal bowling experiences.

segments.title: Bowling scoring: strikes, spares, and perfect games
segments.summary: The hosts explain frame structure, strikes and spares with bonus points, the tenth frame, and the 300 perfect game. They note that computerized scoring has changed how people understand the game.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief break before the next section on bowling gear.

segments.title: History of bowling balls
segments.summary: Early balls were made of lignum vitae wood. Rubber balls followed, then the mineralite process from the 1910s. Later balls used plastic, polyurethane, and resin. The reactive resin cover of the 1990s changed the game, and perfect games jumped from 905 in the 1969 season to 34,470 thirty years later. Regulation size and weight limits are covered.

segments.title: Pins, lanes, and lane construction
segments.summary: Pins were once solid maple and have been glued in sections since the 1950s. Lanes were originally built from pine and maple boards and are now synthetic, reportedly made from phenolic resin.

segments.title: Lane oil patterns
segments.summary: Lanes are coated in mineral oil in patterns. House oil is forgiving for amateurs, while PBA patterns, often named after animals or past bowlers, are harder. A Chris Paul pattern is mentioned.

segments.title: Bowling shoes and other equipment
segments.summary: Rental bowling shoes are described as slip-and-grip shoes that are ugly and uncomfortable. Other gear includes wrist braces and rosin bags, and the ball-return air blowers are mentioned.

segments.title: History of pin boys and early pin machines
segments.summary: Human pin boys set and cleared pins by hand. Later mechanical helpers were used. Fred Schmidt's automatic pin setter was bought by AMF in 1941, and AMF built about 40,000 machines in the 1950s. This was called rhythm bowling.

segments.title: How the automatic pin setter works
segments.summary: The sensors, backstop, sweep, conveyor, accelerator and ball return, spotting tongs, pin elevator with buckets, and centering wedges are described in order. The hosts recommend online animations and live-action videos.

segments.title: Bowling origins and early history
segments.summary: Bowling-like games may be ancient, with possible Egyptian and medieval lawn bowling roots and German religious roots. Ten-pin's origin is uncertain, and a rumor says the tenth pin was added to avoid nine-pin gambling bans. The ABC was formed under Joe Thum.

segments.title: Bowling's popularity, money, and decline
segments.summary: Action bowling in New York involved gambling and the Mafia. Don Carter got a million-dollar contract in 1964. The PBA was bought in 2000 for five million dollars. Bowling alleys and regular bowlers declined sharply, and a comeback is starting.

segments.title: Seven-ten split and closing
segments.summary: The seven-ten split is rare, reportedly done only four times on televised pro tournaments. Anthony Newer is mentioned as the most recent bowler to convert it. The episode closes with the hosts' plans to go bowling again.

segments.title: Listener mail: pronouncing -shire
segments.summary: Teresa from Melbourne, Australia, explains that county names ending in -shire rhyme with 'beer' when used as a suffix, using Worcestershire and Oxfordshire as examples.
